utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal next with the Status Conference. We are in open session. Is there any reason why we shouldn't remain in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not that I can think of, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll remain in open session. We've had the letter now or a copy of the letter from the Defence to the Prosecution setting out matters they wish to raise. It may be convenient to start with the Prosecution. Let us see where we are. Can I, before we do that, summarise my note of progress to date? Totalling the number of days sat, the total, in all, is about 42 days, allowing, of course, for half days and that sort of thing, and we have, during that time, completed 32 witnesses. The progress is slow. We don't necessarily criticise anybody at this stage for that, but we have to bear it in mind for the future. I think things are speeding up. At least in the last week or two, they seem to have been speeded up. But looking at your overview, Mr. Nice, dealing with the above-line witnesses, it seems that you have identified some 150 witnesses remaining, according to my calculations, in that category. Of the various categories, again according to my note, and it may not be totally accurate, of the 70 witnesses in category A, that is the victims and witnesses from the villages and municipalities, who could testify about the accused, it appears you've called about 15 out of a possible 70-odd. You call six international military personnel and monitors out of a total of 30. None of the nine witnesses on the international armed conflict in category C, three of the six witnesses, and 4 out of 74 witnesses to the attacks on the villages in category E. Again, that's not a precise figure but it gives one a rough idea. That means we have a substantial way to go, despite having spent four months. Again, the parties are not to be criticised for that because I've been engaged on another case and that means we have to sit half days. As always in this Tribunal, there are other cases which the Trial Chamber has to deal with, and plenary. So one can't sit through as one would in a national jurisdiction. Perhaps you could tell us how you see the matter progressing in order that we deal with it as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. We're sorting out a printing and copying oversight. I'll explain exactly how I see things progressing. First of all, it's clear that the time that the trial will take is determined by the fact that there is nothing that the Defence can admit, the fact that it appears every witness has to be cross-examined and the length of cross-examination, that is now out of our hands. It is a matter that the Trial Chamber can deal with, and as I think I suggested before, given that the Prosecution has, I think, achieved now the maximum efficiency and economy in the presentation of the evidence in chief, it would be open for the Chamber to require of the Defence, before they cross-examine, an indication of what the objectives of the cross-examination are. It can be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for us, Mr. Nice, if you forgive my saying so. There is one matter that is within your control, and that is the number of witnesses and the amount of evidence which you are going to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour says that that's a matter for you and I must deal with that, because throughout this trial I have respected and reflected at every turn, by myself and by my colleagues, the fact that the Chamber does not value interruptions in the same way as I don't like making them. Therefore, I have kept and we have kept to an absolute minimum, objections about relevance, objections about the production of documents and so on. We have done that for several reasons but not least is because that appears to be, and understandably so, the choice of the Trial Chamber. But if the reality is that time is being taken too little value by excessive cross-examination, then it is appropriate for me to mention it, and it would be wholly wrong for the Prosecution to be under any pressure to reduce the amount of material it is entitled and obliged to present by reason of factors outside its control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have that matter fully in mind. I had in mind to require you to finish this case by Christmas. That would have given you eight months. But the fact is that time is being taken up in cross-examination and that, of course, is outside your control. I note that typically a witness is longer in cross-examination than he is in chief, which is unusual. The usual experience is the other way around. Now, those are matters which we have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I turn to the number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come to the number of witnesses, I think the plan that I have in mind will help you. The crime base, that is the last category of witnesses as we've ordered them in the overview, the village witnesses, the crime base is not something that can now be dealt with on the dossier approach as we have originally planned, but in light of the decision of the Chamber is a matter that we can deal with, we believe, very expeditiously. So what I have in mind is the following: Efforts that were being directed towards preparing dossiers for presentation in Court, on the basis of witness statements and exhibits and so on, are now being refocused on a broadly similar exercise but where one of the principal focuses of the exercise will be the possible reliance on prior testimony, either of witnesses on our list or indeed of witnesses who can give evidence and who gave evidence in other cases on the same villages. Those conducting this exercise will, of course, plan to deal with a village not only by prior testimony but, of course, by the testimony that comes in from witnesses who have already given evidence and from witnesses who will be coming to give evidence on other topics. For example, direct evidence about one or another of the defendants. My forecast is that by probably October or thereabouts, it should be possible for me to have a summary, it may not be a summary that anybody else will want because if it's not going to be agreed it's not going to be of much use, but I will have a summary that will identify the limited number of prior testimonies per village or municipality, and the very limited number of witnesses, if any, additional to those who have already given evidence, that would be required to establish a crime base for a municipality or a village. Now, when that exercise is done, and in a sense it can't be done until we've got a better idea of what the intervening witnesses will provide in relation to crime base, but when it's done and in light of the ruling that the Chamber has given about prior testimony, it will be open, of course, to the Defence to seek leave to cross-examine those who gave prior testimony, but as I read the Trial Chamber's decision, whether they are entitled to cross-examine will be a matter for the Trial Chamber. So my intention is to put all the material about the villages to the end of the trial because so much of the material that covers it will already have come in in other ways, along the way to identify precisely the prior testimonies that we would seek to put in, giving the Defence an opportunity to argue were those witnesses should, if that's their case, come to give evidence, and in the light of the decision that the Chamber would then make about prior testimony, we would be in a position, no doubt, to summarise the prior testimony, because reading prior testimony is a long and unappealing task, we could summarise it so that the Chamber would then have for the crime base documents of the general kind rendered admissible by your decision, summary, as it may well be, of prior testimony, and such limited number of witnesses as in our judgement would then be required to prove the various counts on the indictment. Now, that is my plan. That means that I and the Chamber or we and the Chamber can focus on all the other categories of evidence first. Picking out international armed conflict, it's always possible, in light of recent decisions in this building, that that matter may become more easily resolved and, in any event, it's a matter that may be substantially resolved by the submission of documentary material, as was done in the Blaskic case. So far we've called no individual witness in that category, though we, of course, intend to do so, but note that other evidence of other witnesses does, of course, touch on that issue and can be accumulating so that decisions about that can be made a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the effect of that is of the nine witnesses who you have at the moment, a number you would anticipate not having to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be the case. My very approximate calculation, done with the assistance of Mr. Lopez-Terres, who has, in general terms, been preparing lists and liasing with those who produce witnesses for us, is that there is something in the order of 70 or 80 witnesses above the line from the other categories whom we are likely to wish to call. Say 80 witnesses. Our present rate of producing evidence in chief is that the witnesses last between one and two hours. Some of those witnesses include witnesses who inevitably will be long, other witnesses who will be substantially shorter. Yesterday's witness I think I accomplished in 40 minutes, and if we hadn't been introducing documents it could have been done in 20 minutes, I think, or half an hour. Take two hours as an average for 80 witnesses, 160 hours, divide by 5 for the number of hours in a full Court day. That's a little over 30 days. Six weeks, seven weeks for the evidence in chief, and although, of course, some regard has to be paid to the overall time limit, the time taken by a case, some regard must also be taken when comparing the length of these trials with other trials to the real time taken, and it is my submission that that is not by any means an excessive amount of time to need for a case like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, just let me comment that speaking for myself entirely, if you were to call in a case of this sort a hundred witnesses, I don't think that could be objectionable by any standards. I think that was the figure which the Blaskic Prosecution called, about that. If you were able to do it in 30 days, again, nobody could complain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. Can I -- while we're dealing with the Court's powers, just take us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to -- while you're dealing with witnesses, in your overview, is it possible to reduce the number or produce a document? You produced one amendment on the 11th of May, which rather increased the number. I wondered if there had been any developments since then which we could be told about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There have been no developments to reduce the size of the overview and its general shape. We have produced, and I think they're now available for distribution, a list of witnesses which I hope you'll find helpful and encouraging. Perhaps I can distribute that and then come back to the point I want to make in the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: What is this list exactly? We have now in this list the witnesses to be called until what? Is it limited in time or what? Fifty-two witnesses. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid how long these witnesses will take is substantially out of my control. These 52 witnesses, on my calculation, would take in chief for their evidence 52 times 2.100 divided by 5, 20 days in chief. I can't say how long they'll take overall. But in answer to Your Honour's question, there are a couple of points I want to make. This is both a list of the witnesses we intend to call and we put as a hope or approximation before Christmas. You will see that at the end of the list, the second sheet, there are six names listed with the word "transcript" beside them, and the view is taken that those are witnesses whose evidence may properly be read in either summarised or in full from the transcript, to the considerable saving of time. I come back to the list as it reads. Our concern is, of course, both to present our case but to reflect the needs of the Chamber and the difficult job the Chamber has. Our perception is that it must be easier for the Chamber to have a varied diet but, nevertheless, a sensible diet of witnesses so that we have, generally speaking, interspersed the witnesses we believe to be long witnesses around witnesses who we believe can be taken much more swiftly. So for example, without reading names out, number 4 is likely to be a lengthy witness, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination for number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And number 1 too?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 1 has, but I think the forecast of the time required is about a day, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's not clear to me. You intend to complete your case with these witnesses? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the next 52 witnesses, but I'll explain my position more fully after that. Number 4, I think, would be a lengthy witness. Number 20, too early to identify the witness but would be lengthy. Number 25, an expert. Number 28, 38, and number 40 will be probably longer witnesses. Many of the other witnesses would be short witnesses, and I would still hope very much that we can achieve a figure of between one and two hours for examination-in-chief, even for the longer witnesses and particularly for the experts, because I believe that it is possible, by the techniques we are using and by appropriate use of skills, to get the material across to you very swiftly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, like Judge Robinson and I listening, you are creating an adversarial expectation. Of course, we are quite ready to follow you if you are also ready to give us sufficient elements to support what you are telling us, because you are not only speaking for yourself, you are telling things to the Chamber. So are you intending to still call 80 witnesses, if I followed you properly, that is, in addition to the witnesses we've already heard, you intend on calling another 80 witnesses, and out of these 80 witnesses, 50 are now on the list that you showed us. So this is the first thing that I should like to really clear up. The second thing, you intend to call another 80 witnesses, and you have given us a list of 50 out of these 80 now. Then you also said that you intend to begin with categories A and B and to leave other categories following, in particular, category E, for the end of your case. Did I understand you properly? Categories by villages. You also told us that you intend using transcripts and particularly summaries of transcripts. Personally, I do not think it is quite a good idea. I do not think it would really be good to go into summaries. I think the transcripts should be used or produced such as they are, rather to avoid any controversies arising from summaries. But could you please clarify these points which I have just raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct in all particulars save one, that I am certainly not in a position to identify at this stage precisely how many witnesses I intend to call, whether it's 80 or whether it's more or less, for two reasons: First, as I have already explained, the village crime base evidence may require additional witnesses, some; second, because of the other witness was -- well, there are three reasons, but the second reason is because of the other witnesses on the list that I haven't listed in this first 52, we'll make our minds up about our need to call them as the case unfolds, and it may be that we'll need to call another 20; it may be that we will be able to reduce that number in light of the way the case develops. It has to be borne in mind, and I make this point so that it's not overlooked, that things may arise, as indeed they did this morning in a particular setting, where witnesses have to be added to the list. As this morning's private session revealed, I have to add a witness, at the very least, for cross-examination purposes. So this is not a final list or anything like it, but I am very hopeful that this list will substantially deal with all aspects of the case, apart from those categories that Judge Bennouna correctly explained I had omitted expressly from this list. Can I respectfully take you at this stage, because there is a way in which the Prosecution and the Chamber can, to some degree, work together, it may be, can I take you respectfully to 73 bis (D), which is the Trial Chamber's powers to reduce -- or may call upon the Prosecutor to reduce the number of witnesses if it considers that an excessive number of witnesses are being called to prove the same facts. Where witnesses cross so many boundaries of evidence and aren't, for example, the ten witnesses who prove this particular killing or the ten witnesses who prove that particular destruction of a house, it's an unreal exercise to do this, in a sense, in advance. Our position is that it is too early for the Chamber to be making any orders on us at this stage, and it would be wrong to do so. But given the summaries that we produce that identify topics in numbered paragraphs, it is, of course, the easiest thing in the world both for us to forecast what we need from a witness, where we say, "The witness can speak of 20 paragraphs. We're only going to these two paragraphs in the middle," and we'll take evidence for ten minutes and then to sit down, and it's also possible for the Chamber to indicate, when it's appropriate and safe for the Chamber to do so, that to call any more witnesses on that particular crystallised and carefully identified topic would be excessive, and we will, of course, be responsive to that, subject only to the concerns we've raised earlier about the difficulties that the Chamber has in making provisional, factual findings. But subject to that and that matter having been dealt with in some way and at some stage, if the Chamber looks at a witness statement or a summary and says, "Well, the Chamber doesn't need to hear any more on that topic," then we pass on to the next one. We've made it clear, right from the beginning, that our aim is to keep the Chamber's time full of evidence, and we are prepared in that -- with that in mind, we are prepared to have as many witnesses as is necessary here and lined up, even if each of them is only going to give a very short amount of evidence. So that's the plan. You asked me what the plan is. I am hopeful, especially if the acceleration that, subject to the last witness, we've seen, if an acceleration continues, I'm hopeful, indeed, that these witnesses can be dealt with by Christmas, and I'm hopeful that that would leave a small and manageable amount of the case left. But these time estimates are necessarily extremely approximate. As to His Honour Judge Bennouna's point about transcripts being read, not summarised, we are entirely in the Court's hand, as we are in the Court's hand as to whether if it decides it wants transcripts read in full, it would prefer them read publicly or whether it would be content to read them privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I imagine the latter. If we're trying to save time, we would certainly do so. We will have to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me. I must say that I never spoke about reading, I never mentioned the words "reading of transcript". I was speaking about the tendering of transcripts, so I think that is a misinterpretation on your part, Mr. Nice, of what I said. Let us make it quite clear. I never spoke about reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other matter which you raise is the total number of witnesses and the time. Of course, we recognise that these are all matters which may change and change from day to day. But what we have in mind and what is our responsibility is the overall size of the case and also the length of it, and both of those must be within manageable proportions. I must say, again speaking for myself, the outline which you mentioned, Mr. Nice, does seem to be manageable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if I can assist further on this topic at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should add this, that we have already identified one topic and indicated that we required no further evidence upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and we will do so again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you very much. I don't know if I can help further at this stage. This list is responsive, in part -- well, we're going to prepare it in any event -- but it was responsive to the Defence request. I hope it helps them. They wanted the whole list. I was always prepared to give it. As to the witnesses available for the first fortnight, I can simply tell the Court and my friends opposite that all we do is we try and batch witnesses so that they aren't greatly inconvenienced by being kept waiting, and anything that can be told to us about how long witnesses will take will better ensure that that there are no gaps and, likewise, better ensure that witnesses are not kept too long. At the moment, we are working on the basis of experience, how long each witness has been cross-examined, and having to make our calculations, save when we specifically discovered that it is expected that a witness will take a long time. But the more information, the better for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May I simply inquire at this point, I don't want to interrupt the Prosecutor's presentation, is this approximately the order you intend to call, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is indeed the order we intend, but the order that we intend is frequently something, as the Court will recognise, that we can't deliver for all sorts of reasons, but we'll do our best to stick to this order or approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, you have made a very useful suggestion, and that is referring to 73(D), which we are very familiar with, we know it so well that we have not, up until now, imposed it upon you, but in order to implement it, you need to help us, and that is, inform us, because you are the one who has the information about the witnesses who are coming and the counts, factual points that they are being called to testify on. So to help us, it is not small summaries that do not inform us about anything. I have already been able to comment on it, because on the basis of a summary, we don't know exactly what the witness is going to say and we do not wish to take the responsibility of asking you to scratch from the list such and such a witness. However, on the other hand, could you give us, well in advance and using the team that are not going on holiday, could you give us, well in advance, I don't know how to call them, but the basis of your examination-in-chief, that is, the points on which you are going to call those witnesses to testify on? This is a technique that has functioned well, but we usually get it just on the eve of the appearance. So could you give us a kind of dossier this time regarding the contents of the testimony of these witnesses, which would help us to work in advance, and I think that would help the Defence as well, and to tell us that -- then we would be able to see whether there is repetition or whether it is absolutely necessary. This would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I regret, I think, probably not. This technique that I introduced outside the rules to assist reflects the reality of calling witnesses in these cases, which is as follows: The witnesses are seen at various stages in the last four years, I suppose, and statements are taken from them. They may be seen more than once, but nearly all of them are hundreds of miles away, and contacting witnesses is a difficult exercise which is very time consuming. When a witness comes to give evidence, he comes the night before, and the procedures that we adopt are to take his material, such as it is, and it's not just statements, it may be quite a volume of material, and to summarise that material and to discuss it with him, of course, and correct, amend, and change it. That's the reason the summaries inevitably come late, and I am quite sure that there are simply not the resources to provide a summary of that detail earlier or to provide two summaries. The Defence have the material that provides the outline, the first outline of the witnesses' testimony, but the summaries which reflect all the additional things that they can say and all the changes, if any, that they want to make, can only come when they are here in The Hague. We, therefore, have a batch of witnesses. Say I have five witnesses on a Monday for that week -- well, five witnesses on a Friday, because typically, of course, we get people in on a Friday, work with them over the weekend, and then present them on the Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Yes, you might have Tuesday and Wednesday's summaries ready by Monday, but it's simply not possible to have them ready earlier than that. Then the next batch of witnesses may come in on a Monday or Tuesday typically for the second half of the weekend, and so they then get worked on on Tuesday and Wednesday, and they can't be available until either the day before or a couple of days before they give evidence. So that I'm afraid to say, pleasant and helpful to all of us, though it would be, to have detailed summaries at an earlier stage, I'm afraid it isn't going to be possible because the resources aren't there, and, indeed, it wouldn't be appropriate to go and -- it wouldn't be helpful to go and see the witnesses, even if we had all these teams of people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, I'm interrupting you, and I apologise for that. You are not obliged. You have a detailed summary on the basis of which you are going to conduct the examination-in-chief, but what you could give us is a scheme, a more detailed one than the summaries that we have now, bearing in mind that this scheme, the contents that you know from the information you have collected, will not be definitive. We understand very well that you bring the witness, you specify with him the questions, and you base yourself on a document listing a certain number of points. This is a method that has produced very good results, and everyone is appreciative of this. But perhaps you could work in advance on this witness to give us an outline of the contents of the testimony, because you know that because you're calling them to testify on such and such an aspect, and I think that that is possible. I don't know whether you have the material means to do it, in view of the number of your responsibilities, and whether you have the necessary teams to do this, but in any event, I believe that you could do something in between the small, current summaries that we have and the final document that you use to conduct the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I regret the resources at my disposal, I think, would not make that possible. It's a matter of -- there are not limitless resources here. The summarising exercise is not done by investigators, it's done by lawyers, and the lawyers typically work, whatever their obligations, most evenings and all weekends, and the present tasks that we have occupy all our time. There is also the reality that to provide detailed earlier summaries would be duplicative and, in a sense, dangerous, because if it's done a month or two months before the witness comes, first of all, you have to revisit all the area, reread all the material, so you're doubling up the work, and you run the risk that some of the material that you ought to research to do the job properly will be missed between the two periods or will occur between the two periods and the search engines or whatever else are employed will have to be reused. I'm afraid, my judgement is, that I won't have time to do it. Let me make it quite plain. If I can, if I can in any way deploy my resources to make earlier summaries or earlier draft summaries available, then I'll do so. But I certainly am not in a position to undertake that because I don't believe I can deliver it. Within the way I work, within the way we have to work with the production of witnesses by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, we do provide the summaries at the earliest opportunity, and, of course, the Defence are in a position themselves to review in advance the statements they have of these witnesses, they know now the order, and to know in advance what's coming. Come to that, since we've always made it clear that we are happy for the Chamber to have witness statements if they want them, the Chamber may itself have resources that can, in some way, summarise, beyond the short summaries, what the witness can say. But on that, of course, I'm otherwise ignorant. The Chamber can be quite sure that if there's any deployment of our resources that will make life easier and more efficient, then I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stein, we have your letter of yesterday's date, setting out various matters. Unless there's anything you want to say about what's been said so far, it may be convenient to deal with the letter. I hope we can do it before the adjournment, although that may be overly optimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We are going to end up paying for everyone's dinner if we try to do it by 1.00, because I will have more stops from the reporters and the Court, but I will try. Let me preliminarily observe that the Prosecution's best witnesses are behind them now. That was the order of the Court, and I think it's an important observation to make. Also, something I've harped on continually, the more we know in advance, the better and quicker we are able to style our examinations, hence, although we gritted our teeth and are bearing the process by which the witnesses are led through direct examination, it has produced shorter direct examinations, and the sooner we know, by the offer of proof or summary, what the witnesses are going to say, it helps us, because it shows clearly what part of the witness's statement or testimony the Prosecution is going to function on. So we could ask, and I'm skipping way head, if Your Honour could impose on my colleagues a 24-hour obligation, which you had suggested but we now make the case, that we have the offers of proof 24 hours in advance, it would help us tremendously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the difficulty of imposing it is that there is the physical difficulty of the witness not being here, and that is where being an international court has its problems. We would encourage 24 hours, but I think to impose it may meet the response that there won't be any summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, we wouldn't want that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. But I'm sure the Prosecution have heard what you've said and clearly it is in everybody's interest that the summaries are available as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The next most important thing to observe, based on what I heard my colleague say, is that the Court is going to be, as we march forward, dealing with affidavits which you suggest in your Tulica decision, as well as the use of prior testimony, all of which we have discussed a lot, and I'm not going to repeat that ground, except I do want to observe one point, if I may. With the use of affidavits, which you are allowed, obviously, to use and with the use of the Aleksovski decision with regard to prior testimony, you will have a relatively anomalous situation in that much of your testimony from the Prosecution and presumably the Defence will be in those formats. Now, that's certainly consistent with the rules, but I want to observe, if I may, that that does not give you, in large chunks, the ability to see, hear, and focus on the presentability, credibility of a live witness. That's an obviously statement. The more we rely on the cold record the more anomalous the situation may appear. At some point, of course, Your Honours make a judgement as to balancing that. That's purely an observation on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, of course we have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, Judge, most important, if I may -- it please the Court, is our request at 4, which is the request which we have made consistently to the Office of the Prosecutor for the milinfosums, the battalion records, the war diaries, the radio logs, all of which were mentioned in testimony, all of which are important relative to specific instances, the blockade, the issues that have come up and which I think Your Honours have found useful. You saw the Prosecution's use of those milinfosums, which are a tremendous ongoing recordation of what happens, and we have, as I note in my letter, the Prince of Wales -- the Cheshire, rather, Regiment fairly well in hand. The Prince of Wales replaced the Cheshires and the Coldstream Guards were involved as well. I believe the Prosecution has these already. Certainly we can use whatever processes are available to us to get them but it seems like an awful lot of work. If the Prosecution has them, they're efficacious and helpful to all parties, if they would turn them over to us so we could be better prepared to present for you the evidence from our point of view. I'm given to understand that Mr. Dooley's diary which is in their position is no more legible to them than us and I accept that. Again, I want to repeat what I've said often. I'm asking for this submission and for this information not on a reciprocal discovery basis but instead under the doctrine of completeness because it's already in their hands. They're using it, and it's for that reason that we're proceeding. I believe, if I may move on, paragraph 5 is self-explanatory. I raise it more as a caution for the other side. I also believe we've reached an agreement that the Prosecution will give us their exhibit list. The manner in which the exhibits are coming in, the Z list being out of chronological sequence, I want to be sure that we're operating from the same page. I don't think that's something we need dwell on. The issues raised in paragraphs 7 and 8 are troubling for us. Your Honours have, in the past, intervened on our behalf and, in fact, Your Honour invited the Registry, in an order dated January 13, to provide us with the transcripts of all public sessions in the Aleksovski, Blaskic, Kupreskic, and Furundzija case, and we have been trying to get those transcripts in the first place and it is not easy for a variety of reasons. Similarly with the exhibits in Blaskic. The first step, and we had a meeting yesterday with the registrar, the first step is just getting the witness list and the exhibits list, because then we can carve out which are protected witnesses or confidential witnesses from our requests and make them separate. The other problem is even though a transcript is "public", that doesn't necessarily make it available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stein slow down, please? Could Mr. Stein be asked to slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Hopefully by 27 August we will have the lists, but I'm concerned that we won't have what we need. Mind you, the Office of the Prosecutor has all of the transcripts in all of the cases and all of the exhibits in all of the cases. The second and more fundamental problem that we have not been able to resolve with the Registrar is that the exhibits themselves from Blaskic, which are relevant to this case, the copying of them and the manpower is apparently a problem. We have offered to send secretaries or paralegals over to do that task but that offer was not met with an acceptance. I asked the Court in a benign way to again solicit the registrar. It is obvious that this case could be over by the time we get some of the records and that wouldn't be fair to anyone, the Court or us. Moreover, should the Prosecution or the Defence wish to use any of the transcripts in an affirmative way in lieu of testimony, if we have them ahead of time we can make a judgement whether we object or not. So I hark to the theme I've hearkened to from the beginning: The more we have, the shorter our job will be and the easier it will be to produce evidence of an important nature to the Court. On a more ticklish subject is that which we raise in paragraph 8, the private testimonies of Court witnesses in Blaskic, (redacted) (redacted). We ask the Court to solicit the Trial Chamber in Blaskic to consider releasing those under the same provisions that we have always operated under, the protective order issued by Your Honour some time ago. Again, item 9 is self-explanatory. I don't think we can use it in this courtroom, but that's the blowup that was -- the diorama that was used, I think successfully, in the Blaskic case. I want to raise one point -- actually, two more points. We have -- and I say this -- I don't want to end on a bad note this summer, but we have been constantly scolded or lectured by Mr. Nice relative to a variety of things. I take the Biblical incantation to turn the other cheek which we've done, and I will continue to do save one point. Any witness who takes the stand subject, employed by the Prosecution or not, is subject to challenge, and his bias, her interest, or her motive is subject and fair game. So I just want to make that undeniable and clear what our position is relative to calling members of the Prosecution team or any other witness to the stand. You also asked, Your Honour, in your order when we were discussing where we would proceed, to discuss -- you invite us to discuss the state of the case and deal with any matters which the Defence or the accused may want to raise concerning their detention. I'd like to think that their detention doesn't include us and we may go home for the summer. I think that's all I have. I have three minutes to spare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I have anything particularly to add first, because I want to contribute to the atmosphere to be productive. However, the problem which my colleague Bob Stein mentioned, the process of receiving the materials from other cases is really complicated. It is not that somebody is not doing their job or not willing to contribute, but it is, technically speaking, very, very painful and very, very complicated. We do hope, according to the last information, that we will be able to have at least the majority of those materials from other cases before we resume on -- for the September part of our job. But that could be a glitch, and it is certainly one of the causes why we are not able sometimes to predict how long our cross will need or to discuss the other side, possible stipulations, and it does cause many practical problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If it would help on this issue, Judge, I've prepared a summary of the public transcript requests that we've made of the Registrar and the date, similarly the missing exhibits by case. It's over-inclusive because of the confidential nature. If I may share that with everyone, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would hand that round, please. Would the usher get those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's one. There's another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Stein, so that we have it in mind, your requests relate to the Blaskic material, including the private session material of Court witnesses, and you are formally requesting those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asking us to take steps to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am. It also involves Kupreskic, Judge, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I have made an inquiry of the registrar, and I'm told that it is hoped that the material will be available during the recess but, of course, it does leave the matters you raise in paragraph 8 in relation to the Court witnesses, and that is something which this Trial Chamber will have to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Additionally, I don't know the Prosecution's position on our request, paragraph 4, relative to the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was going to raise that with them. Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps it will help if I deal with exhibits a bit more generally. Core documents, I've tried to agree to those with Mr. Sayers. There were a number of objections to core documents by the Defence, and I haven't discussed it with Mr. Kovacic, but I suspect that it will boil down to this: That where the Defence notify us that they assert a document is a forgery or something to that effect, then of course we will go and produce traditional proof of its authenticity, and I suspect that all other documents are capable of being admitted without proof in the core bundle, subject to any arguments about relevance that would be outstanding. Of course, there are some documents where better copies would be desirable and we'll deal with that. Second, and this is more closely connected to the issue in paragraph 4, I've raised with Mr. Sayers and with Mr. Stein recently, I don't think I've raised it had with Mr. Kovacic, not intentionally, just because it hasn't arisen, but I've raised the possibility of making available to the Defence our present library of documents, that is, all the documents we've presently identified but on a reciprocal basis. The Defence could also provide us -- that they could provide us with all the documents they've presently got and then each side could decide which documents it wanted to trouble the Chamber with. That idea is not acceptable, I gather, with the Defence and, therefore, our proposal or consideration of making our documents available to them is not one we wish at the moment to take forward unilaterally. Unless there is any doubt about it, the reason has to be concern about the use, not of course by the lawyers, but the use that may be made of the knowledge of documents that are held on a unilateral basis where the other side's documents have yet to be seen. But that then brings me on to milinfosums and other matters of that sort. We do not have for either most or all of these categories of documents libraries of them. We don't actually have complete, chronological -- we are not the battalion. So that provision of them would, in any event, be difficult, but -- because we can't do it any better than they can. We have some but we don't have all. But in any event, what they are seeking is that which I think the Blaskic Chamber has said they shouldn't be entitled to, which is full disclosure by the back door when they're not prepared to reciprocate and to trigger reciprocal discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, have you given them all the milinfosums and the like that you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I don't think we have given them all the ones that we have and nor do I think they are entitled to them, because they're entitled to those that are relevant to a particular witness's testimony, but there's no doctrine of completeness that says since you have one particular document from a general category, a category that may be authored by all sorts of different people, that they're entitled ipso facto to the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You might like to review that, have a look at them and decide what to hand over and what not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I had considered, incidentally, at an earlier stage for -- maybe ECMM documents where I think we do have libraries, I'm not so sure, whether the Chamber would itself want to have a library of such documents. There seem to be two competing possibilities. One is a Chamber would like to have a continuous record where they exist that it can turn to as a library document and say, "Well, what was this authority saying on this day or that day?" The alternative is perhaps to reflect the views of Judge Robinson on one or two earlier occasions. You might prefer or ask to identify what you would like and not to be burdened with the responsibility of looking at the whole library. I mentioned we will be responsive to the overall view that the Chamber expresses on that. For the time being, we will carry on the policy of producing what we think to be relevant, but we can't always take the different course. That's the position on exhibits. Can I deal with two other things -- three other things? On page 1, the first page with the letter, there's a reference at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, regarding the document question, because you're making many proposals, what is, after all, the final solution to regulate the matter regarding documents, because we must have a clear answer to give to the Defence. What is the most practical solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that the most practical solution is to carry on the way we are doing, that is, to produce exhibits individually through the witnesses. I will be responsive to His Honour Judge May's invitation to reconsider that in relation to any collection of documents that we have, and I will discuss that with my colleagues and we will not burden the Chamber with an excessive number of libraries of documents unless invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, I should like to suggest on practical terms, because we should also like to do that. We believe that Defence should also prepare and submit a similar list to the Chamber, not for all various categories but a list of documents which you intend to produce. So I should like to ask the Defence to also tell us which of the documents did they miss, which they still need. We could also examine, together with the Prosecutor, rather, with the Prosecutor's Office, anything that could be done very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, if it's convenient, deals with unavailable or unwilling witnesses. This is an argument that started weeks if not months ago and is yet to be concluded. It may be the Chamber would prefer not to conclude it today, especially if I can conclude everything else I have to say in about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in due course when it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I -- well, it's due for resolution. Can I explain what the issue is? We've prepared a skeleton argument which touches on a slightly wider issue, the unwilling witnesses, but is specific as to dead witnesses, namely the two witnesses that are referred to there. The skeleton argument was only available this morning, and I'm afraid I didn't get it served on the Defence until rather later than it was actually available. It was available sometime after 9.30. I'd invited them, at an earlier stage, to prepare themselves with the skeleton argument on unavailable or unwilling witnesses generally. I don't think they've done so, but they may be willing to deal with the argument. However, an alternative would be for the Chamber to take the skeleton argument away and for the matter to be argued shortly, sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That seems sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I have attached to the argument a short paper on "Developments of the Law on and Hearsay in Canada", something I promised, something that might be of particular interest to those with common-law experience, so as not to suggest a bias that I have for I have none. It doesn't suggest the resolution of the problem but it's a thinking document. It's a document to help with those arguments that although they perhaps shouldn't use the word "hearsay" do, and it seemed to me might be a useful piece of material for the Chamber to have, and that is available today. Can we, however, argue the point shortly when we return in the autumn? Dealing with the other points raised by Mr. Stein, paragraph 9 would, I think, be extremely unhelpful, to have the three-dimensional diorama used by Blaskic. It was, I think, for some unexplained reason out of scale by a factor of three vertically, so that it made the area resemble a skiing resort, and was stuck with a whole range of flags, and it doesn't cover the whole area. I have, as the Chamber requested, instituted an exercise which will produce, I think it will be, a large-scale map and probably with overlays to reveal troop deployments and possibly troop movements over the relevant period of time, and I hope that will be available by the time we reconvene in September. Dealing with the territory itself, we've written to the Defence some time ago now with our own proposal for any possible judicial view of the area, and there's no urgency about this, but no doubt the Defence will shortly reply with any other locations that they think the Chamber might like to see, and then the document will be available for the Chamber to consider, but I imagine it would be helpful for the Chamber to have it either at the start of the first session in September or possibly earlier, but there it is. As to the point about all witnesses being fair game, I think that's a matter entirely for the Chamber, but I do have a duty, which I will continue to perform, to keep matters within limits and on point. That's all have I to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are there any points that anybody wishes to raise about the conditions of detention? We're prepared to consider anything which anybody wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only one small thing: If you can help, we did inform the Registry, and, of course, since it is more or less a technical safety consideration thing, it was left to be considered; however, it seems there was no result. Because of certain information which the Dutch security got sometime, I don't know, this spring probably sometime, April or May, the safety was really increased. Among other things, the clients are transported from the detention unit to this building in little private vehicles with heavy bulletproof vests, which, of course, we have to accept because it's security and they are the experts on the issue. The problem is they get very warm, and then they are escorted in the same equipment from the entrance of this building up to the detention part attached to the courtroom, and they get wet from sweating. Of course, we are not experts, and I apologise for that, but it's obvious that a heavy-duty bulletproof vest is not needed when entering the building. If something could be done, if you could address the Registry, that somebody should deal with that, that is the only inconvenience they are facing at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you for soliciting, Judge, but we have nothing to raise on behalf of Mr. Kordic. I would accept anything that they have in their library by way of milinfosums, even if it's not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as the matters which Mr. Kovacic raises, they are matters, of course, primarily of security, and the Court must accept what he's ordered in that respect. But we will ensure that the comments are passed on, and, no doubt, those responsible can look at the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. My client is just telling me that it is now okay in the building, but the same applies for their building in the detention centre, because they are travelling from the main entrance to their part and it's also very, very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The comments can be passed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Ms. Somers reminds me that some of the names on the witness list are witnesses who will almost certainly give evidence with full protection; therefore, the list should remain simply with the lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The list is protected. We will adjourn now until September, half past nine on that Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th of September, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
